---
title: "Do the hand-crafted features differ between projects?"
format:
  html:
    code-fold: true
---

Date: 07/08/2026

## GOHREP

**Goal:**

Test whether the twelve hand-crafted image features from
`10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction` differ significantly between the eight
projects the images came from, and measure how large any differences are.

**Hypothesis:**

The features will differ between projects. The dataset pools separate
experiments by different people, on different plants, with different cameras,
exposures and imaging set-ups. So the whole-leaf brightness and colour features
(`leaf_bright`, `mean_green`, `log_gr`) should differ clearly between projects.
The contrast features compare the CDA with its own leaf (`green_gap`, `ent_gap`).
They are normalised by that leaf, so they should be more stable across
projects.

**Rationale:**

This matters for two reasons. First, if the features differ by project, a model
trained on the pooled dataset can partly learn the imaging batch instead of the
cell death. Any accuracy estimate that does not hold out whole projects would
then overstate how well a model works in a new lab or with a new camera. Second,
project is confounded with severity in this dataset. Projects have very
different mixes of scores (`04_project_level_analysis` §5). So a raw difference
between projects could just mean one project's leaves are more diseased. Every
test is therefore run twice, on the raw values and after removing the effect of
severity score. This separates real differences in imaging from differences in
the mix of scores.

Two facts about the data shape the analysis. Crops from the same source leaf
share lighting, plant and tissue, so they are not independent. The independent
unit is the source leaf. `10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction/10b_score_prediction`
§2 makes the same point for cross validation. Also, the projects are very
unequal in size, from 4 to 89 leaves. So the main test is a permutation ANOVA on
leaves, which assumes no distribution and permutes whole leaves. A mixed model,
with crops nested in leaves, is a parametric check.

---

## 1. Setup

### 1.1 Load required packages

```{r}
#| output: false
# 1.1
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(patchwork)
library(here)
# lme4 and randomForest are called namespaced (lme4::lmer,
# randomForest::randomForest) rather than attached, so they do not mask
# dplyr::select etc.
requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)
requireNamespace("randomForest", quietly = TRUE)
```

### 1.2 Helper functions and output folder

```{r}
# 1.2
source(here("src", "data_helpers.R"))
source(here("src", "plotting_helpers.R"))
save_plot <- make_save_plot("11_project_feature_differences")
```

### 1.3 Load the twelve features and attach project labels

The features are not recomputed here. The eleven region features come from the
segmentation cache saved by `10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction` (§4).
Shannon entropy comes from `09_image_entropy`. They are joined exactly as in the
exported feature table (`data/features/cda_image_features.csv`, §4.1 there).
`frac_g_gt_r` is left out, as in the model features of `10b_score_prediction`.

```{r}
# 1.3.1
seg <- readRDS(here(
  "analyses", "10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction", "segmentation_cache",
  "cda_segmentation_metrics.rds"
))
entropy_raw <- readRDS(here(
  "analyses", "09_image_entropy", "entropy_cache", "cda_metrics.rds"
)) %>%
  filter(size == "Raw") %>%
  transmute(image_id, entropy_raw = entropy)

# Feature order and labels are kept identical to
# 10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction §5, so the two analyses' figures can be
# read side by side: CDA (lesion) measures, then whole-leaf measures, then the
# CDA-vs-leaf contrasts and global measures.
feat_order <- c(
  "cda_green", "cda_bright", "cda_green_sd", "cda_bright_sd",
  "mean_green", "leaf_bright", "leaf_green_sd", "sep", "log_gr",
  "green_gap", "ent_gap", "entropy_raw"
)
feat_labels <- c(
  "CDA greenness", "CDA brightness", "Within-CDA greenness variation",
  "Within-CDA brightness variation", "Whole-leaf mean green level",
  "Whole-leaf brightness", "Whole-leaf greenness spread",
  "Whole-leaf greenness bimodality", "Log green-to-red ratio",
  "CDA-leaf greenness contrast", "CDA-leaf entropy difference", "Shannon entropy"
)
names(feat_labels) <- feat_order
```

Each crop's filename is `<SourceBasename>_<Row>_<Col>_<Pos>`. Removing the final
`_Row_Col_Pos` gives the source leaf. `image_info.csv` gives each source leaf's
folder, whose top level is the project. The shared key maps it to an anonymous
label (`Project A`, `Project B`, and so on). This is the same mapping used in
`04_project_level_analysis` §1.5.

```{r}
# 1.3.2
project_key <- load_project_key()
project_lookup <- setNames(project_key$Anon_Label, project_key$Project)

# Path is recorded once per folder in image_info.csv, so it is filled downwards.
# Extensions differ in case between image_info.csv (.TIF) and the crop
# filenames, so the join is on the extension-stripped stem.
leaf_project <- read_csv(
  here("analyses", "01_generate_raw_data", "01_allocation_info", "image_info.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>%
  fill(Path, .direction = "down") %>%
  transmute(
    stem = tools::file_path_sans_ext(Image),
    Project = unname(project_lookup[sub("/.*", "", Path)])
  )

feat <- seg %>%
  select(image_id, score, all_of(setdiff(feat_order, "entropy_raw"))) %>%
  inner_join(entropy_raw, by = "image_id") %>%
  mutate(source = sub("_[0-9]+_[0-9]+_[0-9]+$", "", image_id)) %>%
  left_join(leaf_project, by = c("source" = "stem")) %>%
  mutate(
    Project = factor(Project),
    source = factor(source),
    score_f = factor(score, levels = 0:6)
  )

stopifnot(!anyNA(feat$Project))
cat(sprintf(
  "%d crops from %d source leaves across %d projects; %d features.\n",
  nrow(feat), nlevels(feat$source), nlevels(feat$Project), length(feat_order)
))
```

---

## 2. What is being compared

### 2.1 Crops and leaves per project

Projects differ greatly in size. Project B alone gives 42% of the crops, while
Projects A and F give four source leaves each. The leaf is the independent unit,
so the effective sample size is the number of leaves, not crops. The small
projects are estimated from very few leaves.

```{r}
# 2.1
project_sizes <- feat %>%
  group_by(Project) %>%
  summarise(Leaves = n_distinct(source), Crops = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(`Crops (%)` = round(100 * Crops / sum(Crops), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Crops))
knitr::kable(project_sizes, caption = "Source leaves and crops per project")

# Project colours, shared with 07_visual_complexity's raw-pixel PCA so a project
# keeps its colour across the two ordinations. Those are matplotlib's tab10
# sampled at 8 points (plt.cm.tab10(np.linspace(0, 1, 8)), which skips tab10's
# red and pink), assigned in the same descending crop-count order used there.
project_pal <- c(
  "#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#9467bd",
  "#8c564b", "#7f7f7f", "#bcbd22", "#17becf"
)
stopifnot(nrow(project_sizes) == length(project_pal))
project_pal <- setNames(project_pal, as.character(project_sizes$Project))
```

### 2.2 Severity mix per project (the confound)

Projects have very different mixes of scores. 52% of Project B's crops score 0,
while Project H has almost none. So for any feature that depends on score, a
difference between projects is partly a difference in how diseased their leaves
are. This is why every test below is also run on values adjusted for score.

```{r}
# 2.2
feat %>%
  count(Project, score_f) %>%
  group_by(Project) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = score_f, values_from = pct, values_fill = 0) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Percent of each project's crops in each severity score class")
```

### 2.3 Score adjustment

Adjusting for score subtracts each score's mean value of a feature, taken over
the whole dataset, and keeps what remains. A project difference that survives
this is a difference *at the same severity*. That is the imaging effect of
interest, not a difference in the mix of scores.

```{r}
# 2.3.1
# Residual of each feature after removing the per-score-class mean (a one-way
# fit on score_f). Residuals are formed on the full crop-level data, then
# averaged per leaf below, so a leaf's residual mean is its typical departure
# from what its severity classes alone would predict.
adj_names <- paste0(feat_order, "_adj")
for (i in seq_along(feat_order)) {
  feat[[adj_names[i]]] <- residuals(lm(feat[[feat_order[i]]] ~ feat$score_f))
}
```

```{r}
# 2.3.2
# Leaf-level tables: one row per source leaf, the independent unit. Raw means
# for the unadjusted tests, score-adjusted residual means for the adjusted ones.
leaf_raw <- feat %>%
  group_by(source, Project) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(feat_order), mean), n_crops = n(), .groups = "drop")
leaf_adj <- feat %>%
  group_by(source, Project) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(adj_names), mean), .groups = "drop")
cat(sprintf(
  "Leaf-level tables: %d leaves, median %d crops per leaf.\n",
  nrow(leaf_raw), median(leaf_raw$n_crops)
))
```

---

## 3. Does each feature differ between projects?

### 3.1 Leaf-level permutation ANOVA (primary test)

For each feature, the one-way ANOVA F statistic across projects is computed on
the leaf means. The null distribution comes from randomly reassigning the
project labels *of whole leaves* 9,999 times. Permuting leaves rather than crops
keeps the test valid, because crops from the same leaf are correlated.
Permutation also avoids assuming normal distributions or equal variances. Both
are doubtful with projects of 4 to 89 leaves. The effect size is η², the share
of the variance between leaves that project explains. The twelve p-values are
corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg.

```{r}
# 3.1.1
f_stat <- function(y, g) {
  g <- factor(g)
  group_mean <- tapply(y, g, mean)
  group_n <- tapply(y, g, length)
  ss_between <- sum(group_n * (group_mean - mean(y))^2)
  ss_within <- sum((y - group_mean[g])^2)
  c(
    F = (ss_between / (nlevels(g) - 1)) / (ss_within / (length(y) - nlevels(g))),
    eta2 = ss_between / (ss_between + ss_within)
  )
}

n_perm <- 9999
perm_test <- function(y, g, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  observed <- f_stat(y, g)
  null_f <- replicate(n_perm, f_stat(y, sample(g))["F"])
  # +1 in both numerator and denominator: the observed labelling is itself one
  # of the permutations, so p can never be 0.
  c(observed, p = (1 + sum(null_f >= observed["F"])) / (n_perm + 1))
}
```

```{r}
# 3.1.2
perm_results <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(feat_order), function(i) {
  raw <- perm_test(leaf_raw[[feat_order[i]]], leaf_raw$Project, seed = 100 + i)
  adj <- perm_test(leaf_adj[[adj_names[i]]], leaf_adj$Project, seed = 200 + i)
  data.frame(
    feature = feat_order[i], Feature = unname(feat_labels[i]),
    F_raw = raw["F"], eta2_raw = raw["eta2"], p_raw = raw["p"],
    F_adj = adj["F"], eta2_adj = adj["eta2"], p_adj = adj["p"],
    row.names = NULL
  )
})) %>%
  mutate(
    q_raw = p.adjust(p_raw, "BH"),
    q_adj = p.adjust(p_adj, "BH")
  )

perm_results %>%
  transmute(
    Feature,
    `F (raw)` = round(F_raw, 2), `eta2 (raw)` = round(eta2_raw, 3),
    `q (raw)` = signif(q_raw, 2),
    `F (score-adj)` = round(F_adj, 2), `eta2 (score-adj)` = round(eta2_adj, 3),
    `q (score-adj)` = signif(q_adj, 2)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(`eta2 (score-adj)`)) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = paste(
      "Leaf-level permutation ANOVA of each feature across projects",
      "(9,999 permutations of whole-leaf project labels; q = BH-corrected p)."
    )
  )

cat(sprintf(
  "Significant at q < 0.05: %d/%d features raw, %d/%d score-adjusted.\n",
  sum(perm_results$q_raw < 0.05), nrow(perm_results),
  sum(perm_results$q_adj < 0.05), nrow(perm_results)
))
```

### 3.2 Mixed-model likelihood-ratio tests (parametric companion)

The same question, asked a second way at the level of crops. The leaf is a
random intercept, so the correlation within each leaf is modelled rather than
averaged away. Project is tested with a likelihood-ratio test against the same
model without project. The score-adjusted version adds severity score as a fixed
effect (`value ~ score_f + Project + (1 | leaf)` against
`value ~ score_f + (1 | leaf)`). The effect size is the rise in marginal R² when
project is added, which is the share of the total variance that project
explains. This is a check, not the main test, because the likelihood-ratio
chi-square gives p-values that are too small with only eight groups.

```{r}
#| output: false
# 3.2.1
# Marginal R^2 (Nakagawa): variance of the fixed-effect predictions over the
# total of fixed, random-intercept, and residual variance.
r2_marginal <- function(model) {
  var_fixed <- var(as.vector(model.matrix(model) %*% lme4::fixef(model)))
  var_random <- sum(as.numeric(lme4::VarCorr(model)))
  var_fixed / (var_fixed + var_random + sigma(model)^2)
}

# ML (not REML) fits, since the likelihood-ratio test compares fixed-effect
# structures.
lrt_project <- function(value, with_score) {
  dat <- data.frame(
    value = value, Project = feat$Project, source = feat$source, score_f = feat$score_f
  )
  form_full <- if (with_score) value ~ score_f + Project + (1 | source) else value ~ Project + (1 | source)
  form_null <- if (with_score) value ~ score_f + (1 | source) else value ~ 1 + (1 | source)
  m_full <- lme4::lmer(form_full, dat, REML = FALSE)
  m_null <- lme4::lmer(form_null, dat, REML = FALSE)
  comparison <- anova(m_null, m_full)
  c(
    chisq = comparison$Chisq[2], df = comparison$Df[2],
    p = comparison$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2],
    dR2 = r2_marginal(m_full) - r2_marginal(m_null)
  )
}

lmm_results <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(feat_order), function(i) {
  raw <- lrt_project(feat[[feat_order[i]]], with_score = FALSE)
  adj <- lrt_project(feat[[feat_order[i]]], with_score = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    feature = feat_order[i], Feature = unname(feat_labels[i]),
    chisq_raw = raw["chisq"], df = raw["df"], p_raw = raw["p"], dR2_raw = raw["dR2"],
    chisq_adj = adj["chisq"], p_adj = adj["p"], dR2_adj = adj["dR2"],
    row.names = NULL
  )
})) %>%
  mutate(q_raw = p.adjust(p_raw, "BH"), q_adj = p.adjust(p_adj, "BH"))
```

```{r}
# 3.2.2
lmm_results %>%
  transmute(
    Feature,
    `chi2 (raw)` = round(chisq_raw, 1), `q (raw)` = signif(q_raw, 2),
    `chi2 (score-adj)` = round(chisq_adj, 1), `q (score-adj)` = signif(q_adj, 2),
    `dR2 (score-adj)` = round(dR2_adj, 3)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(`chi2 (score-adj)`)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Mixed-model likelihood-ratio tests of the project term (7 df).")

agree <- sum((perm_results$q_adj < 0.05) == (lmm_results$q_adj < 0.05))
cat(sprintf(
  "Permutation and mixed-model tests agree on %d/%d features (score-adjusted, q < 0.05).\n",
  agree, nrow(perm_results)
))
```

### 4.1 Feature distributions by project

The distributions of all twelve features over crops, split by project. Each
feature has its own y-axis, because the features have different scales.

### 4.2 Project signatures at matched severity

Each project's mean score-adjusted leaf value for each feature, in standard
deviations of the distribution across leaves. This puts all twelve features on
one scale. The pattern of how a project departs from the dataset average can
then be read as its signature.

```{r fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
# 4.2
# z-scores are taken over leaves (the independent unit), then averaged within
# project, so a large project does not shrink its own z simply by dominating the
# dataset mean.
z_leaf <- leaf_adj
z_leaf[adj_names] <- scale(as.matrix(leaf_adj[adj_names]))

project_z <- z_leaf %>%
  group_by(Project) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(adj_names), mean), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_longer(-Project, names_to = "feature", values_to = "z") %>%
  mutate(feature = factor(
    sub("_adj$", "", feature),
    levels = perm_results$feature[order(-perm_results$eta2_adj)],
    labels = unname(feat_labels[perm_results$feature[order(-perm_results$eta2_adj)]])
  ))

p_heat <- ggplot(project_z, aes(x = feature, y = Project, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", z)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B", midpoint = 0,
    name = "Project mean\n(SD of leaf\ndistribution)"
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1, size = 10),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11), panel.grid = element_blank(),
    # Extra left margin so the first rotated label is not clipped when saved.
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 5.5, 5.5, 55)
  )
p_heat
save_plot(p_heat, "project_feature_signature_heatmap.png", width = 9, height = 5.5)
```

```{r}
# 4.2b
# The largest project-to-project gap per feature, in between-leaf SDs, with the
# two projects it separates.
gaps <- project_z %>%
  group_by(feature) %>%
  summarise(
    gap_sd = max(z) - min(z),
    highest = Project[which.max(z)], lowest = Project[which.min(z)],
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(gap_sd))
gaps %>%
  transmute(
    Feature = feature, `Largest gap (SD)` = round(gap_sd, 2),
    Highest = highest, Lowest = lowest
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Largest project-to-project difference per feature, at matched severity.")
```

---

## 5. Do the twelve features jointly separate projects?

### 5.1 Multivariate permutation test

The tests above take one feature at a time. This asks whether the twelve
together separate the projects. It uses a PERMANOVA-style pseudo-F on the
standardised, score-adjusted leaf means, with Euclidean distance and the same
permutation of whole leaves. R² is the share of the total spread that lies
between projects.

```{r}
# 5.1
Z <- as.matrix(z_leaf[adj_names])
pseudo_f <- function(Z, g) {
  g <- factor(g)
  k <- nlevels(g)
  group_mean <- t(sapply(levels(g), function(l) colMeans(Z[g == l, , drop = FALSE])))
  group_n <- as.numeric(table(g))
  grand <- colMeans(Z)
  ss_between <- sum(group_n * rowSums((group_mean - matrix(grand, k, ncol(Z), byrow = TRUE))^2))
  ss_within <- sum((Z - group_mean[g, , drop = FALSE])^2)
  c(
    F = (ss_between / (k - 1)) / (ss_within / (nrow(Z) - k)),
    R2 = ss_between / (ss_between + ss_within)
  )
}

set.seed(7)
observed_mv <- pseudo_f(Z, z_leaf$Project)
null_mv <- replicate(n_perm, pseudo_f(Z, sample(z_leaf$Project))["F"])
cat(sprintf(
  "Multivariate (12 features, score-adjusted leaf means): pseudo-F = %.2f, R2 = %.3f, p = %.4f\n",
  observed_mv["F"], observed_mv["R2"], (1 + sum(null_mv >= observed_mv["F"])) / (n_perm + 1)
))
```

### 5.2 Ordination of leaves by project

PCA of the same standardised, score-adjusted leaf means, coloured by project. If
the projects were interchangeable, their clouds would overlap.

```{r fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.5}
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
# 5.2
pca <- prcomp(Z, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
var_pc <- 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
pca_df <- data.frame(PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2], Project = z_leaf$Project)

# Ellipses are drawn only for projects with at least 8 leaves. A covariance
# ellipse fitted to 4 points (Projects A and F) is arbitrary, so those projects
# are shown as points only.
ellipse_projects <- project_sizes$Project[project_sizes$Leaves >= 8]

p_pca <- ggplot(pca_df, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = Project)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(
    data = filter(pca_df, Project %in% ellipse_projects),
    level = 0.68, linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = project_pal) +
  labs(
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", var_pc[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", var_pc[2]),
    caption = paste(
      "One point per source leaf. Ellipses cover 68% of each project,",
      "and are omitted for the two projects with only 4 leaves."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 12), legend.title = element_text(size = 11))
p_pca
save_plot(p_pca, "project_pca_leaf_means.png", width = 7.5, height = 5.5)
```

### 5.3 Can the project be identified from the features alone?

The same question in practical terms. A random forest is trained to predict the
project from the twelve features of each crop. It uses the same 5-fold cross
validation, grouped by leaf, as
`10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction/10b_score_prediction` §2. So no leaf is
in both the training and the held-out folds. Projects are downsampled to equal
size, so chance is 1/8 = 12.5%, and exact accuracy equals balanced accuracy. A
run with shuffled labels checks for leakage.

```{r}
# 5.3
set.seed(42)
min_n <- min(table(feat$Project))
balanced_idx <- unlist(lapply(levels(feat$Project), function(p) {
  idx <- which(feat$Project == p)
  if (length(idx) > min_n) sample(idx, min_n) else idx
}))
bal <- feat[balanced_idx, ]

K <- 5
set.seed(42)
usrc <- unique(as.character(bal$source))
src_fold <- setNames(sample(rep(1:K, length.out = length(usrc))), usrc)
fold <- unname(src_fold[as.character(bal$source)])

X <- as.matrix(bal[, feat_order])
grouped_cv_accuracy <- function(y) {
  pred <- factor(rep(NA, length(y)), levels = levels(y))
  for (k in 1:K) {
    tr <- fold != k
    model <- randomForest::randomForest(x = X[tr, , drop = FALSE], y = y[tr], ntree = 300)
    pred[!tr] <- predict(model, X[!tr, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  list(
    balanced = mean(vapply(levels(y), function(l) mean(pred[y == l] == l), numeric(1))),
    per_class = vapply(levels(y), function(l) mean(pred[y == l] == l), numeric(1))
  )
}

y_project <- droplevels(bal$Project)
acc <- grouped_cv_accuracy(y_project)
set.seed(9)
acc_shuffled <- grouped_cv_accuracy(factor(sample(as.character(y_project)), levels = levels(y_project)))

cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    "Balanced set: %d crops per project (%d total).\n",
    "Project identification from the 12 features: %.1f%% balanced accuracy",
    " (chance %.1f%%).\nShuffled-label control: %.1f%%.\n"
  ),
  min_n, nrow(bal), 100 * acc$balanced, 100 / nlevels(y_project), 100 * acc_shuffled$balanced
))
data.frame(Project = names(acc$per_class), Accuracy = round(acc$per_class, 3), row.names = NULL) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Held-out project identification accuracy per project (chance = 0.125).")
```

---

## 6. Interpretation and Discussion

- **The features differ between projects, and not only because of the mix of
  scores.** All twelve features differ significantly between projects at the
  same severity (permutation ANOVA on leaves, BH-corrected q < 0.05, §3.1). The
  mixed models on crops agree (§3.2). Only `cda_bright_sd` is not significant
  *before* adjusting for score but is significant after. That is what a severity
  confound looks like when it works against the imaging effect. The tests use
  leaf means and permute whole leaves, so the result does not come from
  treating correlated crops as independent.
- **The effects are large for the appearance and texture features.** At the
  same severity, project explains 26 to 35% of the variance between leaves in
  five features. These are the spread of greenness within the CDA, the spread of
  greenness over the leaf, leaf brightness, the leaf's mean green level and CDA
  brightness (§3.1). The largest gaps between projects reach 2.1 to 2.5 SD of the
  distribution across leaves (§4.2). These features should follow camera,
  exposure and imaging set-up, so differences between projects are expected.
  Projects E and H are at opposite extremes on every brightness feature. They
  differ by about 2 SD in leaf brightness alone.
- **The contrast features are not as stable as expected.** The hypothesis was
  that contrasts between CDA and leaf would be stable across projects, because
  each is normalised by its own leaf. `green_gap` and `ent_gap` still differ
  substantially between projects (η² ≈ 0.26 to 0.28 after adjustment). So
  comparing a lesion with its own leaf removes some of the imaging effect, but
  not all of it. The two features closest to being the same in every project are
  Shannon entropy (η² ≈ 0.08) and greenness bimodality (η² ≈ 0.08 after
  adjustment, down from 0.27 raw). So most of bimodality's apparent difference
  between projects *is* the mix of scores. Bimodality is the feature used to
  detect a CDA in `10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction` §4, which is
  reassuring for that use.
- **Together, the features identify projects strongly.** The multivariate
  permutation test gives pseudo-F ≈ 8.8, with project explaining about 23% of
  the spread between leaves (p < 0.001, §5.1). A random forest identifies which
  of the eight projects a crop came from about 41% of the time, from the twelve
  features alone. Chance is 12.5%, and shuffled labels give 12% (§5.3). For
  comparison, the same features predict the exact severity score about 62% of
  the time in `10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction/10b_score_prediction`. So
  they say a lot about which experiment produced an image, as well as what it
  shows.
- **What this means for modelling.** The features partly reveal the project, so
  a model trained on the pooled dataset can rely on the imaging batch. The cross
  validation grouped by leaf in
  `10_segmentation_and_feature_extraction/10b_score_prediction` does not protect
  against this. It holds out leaves, not projects, so every held-out leaf has
  leaves from the same project in training. The held-out accuracy of about 62%
  there is therefore performance within this dataset. Leaving out one project at
  a time would give an honest estimate for a new lab or camera. The same caution
  applies to the deep learning models trained on this dataset.
- **Limitations.** Project is fully confounded with everything that varies
  between experiments. That includes camera, exposure, imaging distance, plant
  batch, growth conditions and infiltration method. So these tests show *that*
  the projects differ, not *why*. Two projects give only four source leaves each
  (§2.1). Their means are imprecise, and they contribute little to the effect
  sizes. The score adjustment uses one pooled mean per score. It removes the
  average effect of severity, but not any difference between projects in how a
  given score looks. That remainder is counted as a project effect by design.
